straitStatus.description: Day 78 of crisis. Strait remains effectively closed (~5% of pre-war traffic per Windward vessel transponder data). Diplomatic arc this week: May 6 Axios reports US-Iran 'one-page memo' close. May 11 Trump rejects Iran's counterproposal as 'totally unacceptable'; Iran vows 'never bow' (insisting on war reparations, full Hormuz sovereignty, sanctions end, frozen-asset release). May 14 Trump-Xi Beijing summit: both leaders jointly agreed Hormuz 'must remain open' and Iran 'can never have nuclear weapons'; Treasury Sec. Bessent (CNBC) said China will 'work behind the scenes' on Iran (China has the greatest interest in reopening given nearly all Iranian crude exports flow there); a vessel was seized near the Strait by 'unauthorized personnel' during the summit. May 15 US thwarted attacks on 3 Navy ships in the Strait and retaliated against Iranian facilities — first direct US-Iran Navy exchange of the crisis. UK announced deployment (drones + fighters + Royal Navy warship) for international defensive mission on May 13. Project Freedom remains suspended (last activity: May 5, 2 ships transited). EIA (May 13): record 8.6 Mb single-week SPR draw, beating Sept 2022's 8.4 Mb prior record. Brent recovered to $111.04 (+8.1% week) after a brief Dubai-Brent inversion on May 14 (Dubai $101 vs Brent $106 — first inversion since crisis onset). HFI/JPM net shortfall remains 8.5 Mbpd; MacroEdge 13.5-14 Mbpd. ~1,550 vessels and 22,500 mariners still stranded. US estimates ~6 months full mine clearance once strait reopens.

alternativeRoutes.description: Now the dominant rerouting path — capacity bottlenecks at East African ports worsening. War-risk surcharge component rising as VLCC rates climb.
Pipeline saturated; cannot compensate for maritime closure. Saudi drone strike on key pumping station temporarily disrupted throughput in mid-April.
Constrained by ongoing Red Sea security risk and Houthi threats; insurance costs rising in tandem with Gulf premiums.

regionalImpact.description: Imports 40% of oil and 30% of LNG via Hormuz. 55 Chinese-flagged ships trapped in Persian Gulf.
Heavily dependent on Middle East oil via Hormuz; supply disruption threatens industrial production.
Import-dependent nation; oil import costs surging, affecting refiner margins and energy sector.
12-14% of LNG sourced from Qatar via Hormuz; alternative sourcing expensive and limited.

~45–50% of crude transited Hormuz pre-crisis (PPAC/Vortexa Q1 2026). ISPRL Phase-1 ~9.5 days at full / ~6 days at March 64% fill; +OMC commercial = ~74 days total national cover. Permitted limited vessel transits through negotiation.

crisisTimeline.title: US thwarts attacks on 3 Navy ships in Strait + retaliates against Iranian facilities
crisisTimeline.description: First direct US Navy / Iranian Navy fire exchange of the crisis. US said it thwarted Iranian attacks on three Navy ships transiting the Strait, then retaliated against Iranian military facilities. UAE simultaneously intercepted two ballistic missiles and three drones launched by Iran the same day — three wounded. Brent closes the week at $111.04, +8.1% week. Crisis enters Day 77.

crisisTimeline.title: Trump-Xi Beijing summit: both agree Strait 'must remain open'; China to work behind scenes on Iran
crisisTimeline.description: Trump and Xi Jinping, meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, jointly published nine commitments including: Strait of Hormuz 'must remain open', Iran 'can never have nuclear weapons'. Xi expressed opposition to any toll or militarization of the Strait, and interest in purchasing more US oil to reduce China's Hormuz dependence. Treasury Secretary Bessent (CNBC): China will 'work behind the scenes to the extent anyone has any say over the Iranian leadership.' China cited as having the greatest interest in reopening — nearly all Iranian crude exports flow to China. Complication: a vessel was seized near the Strait by 'unauthorized personnel' and taken toward Iran during the summit. Saudi June OSP for Asia cut to +$15.50/bbl above Oman/Dubai (from record +$19.50 May). Brent fell from $111 to ~$106 on the news; WTI held above $101. Dubai inverted to $5 discount vs Brent — first since crisis onset.

crisisTimeline.title: EIA: record 8.6 Mb single-week SPR withdrawal — biggest ever
crisisTimeline.description: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (week ending May 8): SPR drew a record 8.6 Mb, beating the prior all-time weekly high of 8.4 Mb set in September 2022. SPR now stands at 384.1 Mb — lowest since October 2024. Commercial crude stocks −4.3 Mb. Refineries ran 16.4 Mbpd at 91.7% capacity utilization (+369 kbpd WoW). The US is bleeding from every barrel source simultaneously to keep products flowing.

crisisTimeline.title: UK deploys drones, fighter aircraft, Royal Navy warship for international Hormuz defensive mission
crisisTimeline.description: Britain announced its first major naval reinforcement of the strait-clearance effort. Signals widening multilateral commitment to securing freedom of navigation independently of US Operation Freedom (which remains suspended). Mine-clearance timeline still ~6 months once strait reopens.

crisisTimeline.title: Trump rejects Iran counterproposal — 'totally unacceptable'; Iran vows 'never bow'
crisisTimeline.description: Iran's response to the May 6 one-page memo framework insisted on war reparations, full sovereignty over Hormuz, sanctions termination, and release of frozen Iranian assets. Trump rejected outright. Tehran officials said Iran would 'never bow.' Brent had retreated $7 (May 6–11) on memo optimism and snapped back, closing the week +8.1%.

crisisTimeline.title: UAE intercepts second Iranian salvo in five days
crisisTimeline.description: UAE defense systems engaged a second wave of inbound Iranian ballistic missiles and drones. Mosaic Strategy continues despite ceasefire framework talks — Iran's decentralized sector commanders maintain attack tempo independent of diplomatic track.

crisisTimeline.title: Axios: US–Iran closing in on one-page memo to end war
crisisTimeline.description: Framework reportedly the closest the parties have been since war began: Iran nuclear enrichment moratorium + US sanctions lift + frozen-asset release + mutual lift of Hormuz transit restrictions. Brent fell from $109 toward $102 over the following five days on optimism — snapped back after Trump's May 11 rejection.

crisisTimeline.title: Iran's largest UAE strike of crisis — Fujairah refinery hit; Project Freedom launches
crisisTimeline.description: Iran fired 12 ballistic missiles, 3 cruise missiles, and 4 drones at UAE on May 4. Iranian drone strike hit a Fujairah oil processing plant, causing a fire and three Indian citizen injuries. Same day, Trump ordered Operation Project Freedom — US Navy mission to escort stranded merchant ships out of the Gulf. 2 vessels transited safely May 5 before Project Freedom was suspended May 6 pending US–Iran maritime agreement. UAE attacked again May 5 and May 8.

crisisTimeline.title: Operation Freedom suspended after 1-ship-in-24h transit print + 24 Mbbl API draw
crisisTimeline.description: Trump abruptly suspended Operation Freedom — the latest attempt to reopen Strait traffic — after market close on May 6. Catalyst: JaguarAnalytics daily transit tracker showed just 1 ship crossing the Strait in the prior 24 hours, and API printed a ~24 Mbbl total-products inventory draw for the week. MacroEdge estimates 13.5–14 Mbpd remaining offline (vs HFI's 11.5) and expects strait normalization no earlier than late summer / fall, citing the IRGC's strategic interest in maintaining long-term Strait control as a revenue stream.

crisisTimeline.title: HFI/JPM: 8.5 Mbpd net shortfall, backwardation pricing 'wrong'
crisisTimeline.description: HFI Research's Jon Costello argues both oil and equity markets are mispriced — the 8.5 Mbpd net shortfall (after 9.5 Mbpd bypass production and 3.0 Mbpd IEA SPR releases) is being absorbed by 7.1 Mbpd inventory draws and 4.3 Mbpd forced demand destruction (JPM, April). Cumulative ~330 Mbbl drawn over Mar+Apr. Dec '26 Brent sub-$80 vs front $110 implies rapid normalization the supply math doesn't support. IEA's 120-day SPR window exhausts ~Jul 9.

crisisTimeline.title: Trump: blockade could last 'months' until nuclear deal
crisisTimeline.description: President Trump tells reporters the US naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue for months absent Iranian nuclear concessions. Polymarket odds for blockade lifted by May 31 collapse to 25% (-35.5pp 7-day); odds of strait traffic returning to normal by May 31 just 16%.

crisisTimeline.title: Brent settles $114 after $126 peak; ceasefire halts 60-day war powers deadline
crisisTimeline.description: Brent retreats to $114.01 settle after intraday spike to $126.41 on Apr 30 (June contract, four-year high). White House confirms ceasefire extension halts Trump's 60-day war powers clock. Crack spreads at fresh highs — gasoline crack at $47/bbl, heating oil at $66/bbl. Dual blockade unchanged.

crisisTimeline.title: Brent intraday $126.41 — highest in four years
crisisTimeline.description: Brent June contract spiked to $126.41 on US-Iran escalation fears before retreating. Bloomberg Hormuz Tracker: only one Iran-linked fuel tanker observed entering Persian Gulf for the day. Commercial transits at near-zero — both Brent and WTI up ~60% since Feb 28.

crisisTimeline.title: Iran offers to reopen Strait if US lifts blockade — nuclear talks set aside
crisisTimeline.description: Tehran's foreign ministry decouples Hormuz from nuclear file. Trump discusses proposal with Rubio and top aides; White House non-committal. ~2,000 ships still stranded in Gulf. Underwriters say transit confidence won't return until 'sustained normal vessel movement, not isolated transits.'

crisisTimeline.title: US intercepts M/V Sevan; Russian superyacht Nord transits unchallenged
crisisTimeline.description: USS-led interception of Panama-flagged propane/butane carrier M/V Sevan in Arabian Sea on suspected Iran-linked cargo. Russian superyacht Nord crossed the Gulf without incident from either navy — selective enforcement signal.

crisisTimeline.title: USS Rafael Peralta captures unidentified Iranian oil tanker
crisisTimeline.description: US Navy seizure inside Persian Gulf — first US destroyer-led capture of an Iranian-flagged tanker within Gulf waters since blockade began Apr 13.

crisisTimeline.title: Trump orders US Navy to destroy Iranian mine-laying boats
crisisTimeline.description: Standing kill order for any Iranian vessel laying mines in strait. US military says full mine clearance — once strait reopens — will take approximately six months. Underwriters cite mine-clearance timeline as gating factor for premium normalization.

crisisTimeline.title: Iran attacks Greek Epaminondas off Oman; seizes MSC Francesca
crisisTimeline.description: Iranian gunboat fired RPGs at Greek-owned Epaminondas despite prior transit clearance, causing significant bridge damage. IRGC also seized Liberia-flagged container ship MSC Francesca. US captured VLCC Majestic X. CENTCOM reports 29 vessels intercepted total. Trump claims blockade costs Iran $500M/day.

crisisTimeline.title: Trump extends ceasefire pending negotiations — Pakistan brokers
crisisTimeline.description: Trump declared ceasefire extension at Pakistan's request to allow Iranian proposal. Naval blockade maintained. US officials gave Iran 3-5 days to engage in talks before resuming strikes. CENTCOM intercepts at 27 vessels. US captures supertanker Tifani in Indo-Pacific.

crisisTimeline.title: US seizes Iranian-flagged vessel; Iran demands release
crisisTimeline.description: US Navy fired on and seized an Iranian cargo ship defying the blockade. Iran demands immediate release as ceasefire deadline looms. Tensions at maximum — traffic through strait at near-standstill (3 vessels/day).

crisisTimeline.title: Iran recloses Strait — fires on ships, 3 vessels attacked
crisisTimeline.description: Iran reversed its reopening after US refused to lift naval blockade. Iranian forces fired on Indian-flagged ships and CMA CGM Everglade (rocket damage). 35 outbound vessels reversed course. 6 stranded cruise ships evacuated through brief window.

crisisTimeline.title: Iran announces strait open during Lebanon truce — short-lived
crisisTimeline.description: Iran declared commercial passage 'completely open' during Lebanon ceasefire. Trump clarified US blockade on Iranian ports remains. Iran cancelled reopening within 24 hours.

crisisTimeline.title: US declares naval blockade of Iranian ports
crisisTimeline.description: After Islamabad talks failed, Trump declared naval blockade preventing ships from entering/exiting Iranian ports. Freedom of navigation maintained for non-Iranian port traffic. Transit dropped from 17/day to 6/day.

crisisTimeline.title: US Navy destroyers enter strait for mine clearance
crisisTimeline.description: First US Navy entry into the strait since hostilities began. Mine clearance operations commence. Transit surges briefly to 17 vessels as ships attempt to exploit ceasefire window.

crisisTimeline.title: Ceasefire agreement reached — Iran charges $1M+ tolls
crisisTimeline.description: Temporary ceasefire agreed. Iran began controlling traffic and charging tolls exceeding $1M per ship. 45 ships transited in first 4 days. Gulf states intercepted missiles hours into ceasefire.

crisisTimeline.title: Iranian attacks on Gulf states surge to monthly high
crisisTimeline.description: Bloomberg Intelligence data shows Iranian attacks spiking. UAE intercepted 537 ballistic missiles, 2,256 drones, 26 cruise missiles cumulatively. Iran's 'Mosaic Strategy' continues.

crisisTimeline.title: Status quo: controlled transit, ongoing negotiations
crisisTimeline.description: Strait under selective Iranian control with ~6% of normal traffic. Trump extended deadline to April 6. Estimated 2000 ships stranded. War risk insurance still 6-7x normal.

crisisTimeline.title: China-Pakistan present 5-point ceasefire initiative
crisisTimeline.description: China and Pakistan jointly present peace proposal including immediate ceasefire, halt to infrastructure attacks, safe passage through Strait, and framework for comprehensive peace.

crisisTimeline.title: Iran selectively allows approved nations to transit
crisisTimeline.description: Iran permits passage for vessels from China, Russia, India, Iraq, Pakistan. Malaysia and Thailand granted access following direct talks. UN humanitarian and fertilizer shipments permitted.

crisisTimeline.title: Trump issues 48-hour ultimatum to open Strait
crisisTimeline.description: Trump warns Iran that power plants will be obliterated unless Strait fully opens within 48 hours. Iran responds with threats to target US/Israeli energy infrastructure and lay sea mines.

crisisTimeline.title: US releases 400M barrels from Strategic Petroleum Reserve
crisisTimeline.description: Largest SPR release in history. Estimated 95 days of supply at current drawdown rate. Global coordinated release with IEA members.

crisisTimeline.title: US Navy deploys carrier strike group to Gulf of Oman
crisisTimeline.description: USS Eisenhower carrier strike group positioned in Gulf of Oman. Additional destroyer deployments to escort allied vessels. Iran IRGC navy conducts counter-exercises.

crisisTimeline.title: Iran restricts Strait of Hormuz transit
crisisTimeline.description: Iran begins controlled transit regime following escalation of US-Iran tensions over nuclear program. Initial blockade affects all non-allied vessels. Oil prices spike 15% overnight.

phases.description: Diplomatic resolution, ceasefire agreement, and physical reopening of strait. China-Pakistan 5-point ceasefire initiative in progress.

Even after strait reopens, it takes 2-3 months for tanker schedules, port logistics, and crude flows to renormalize. Ships need to reposition, insurance rates need to fall, and loading schedules must reset.
Steam crackers and shut-in refineries across Asia need full restart cycles. Naphtha supply chain must rebuild. Force majeures across petrochemical sector will take months to unwind.
Inventory rebuilding, SPR replenishment, insurance rate normalization, and return to pre-crisis pricing. Consensus estimate: September 2026 at the earliest.

recoveryClock.keyInsight: Asia passed the point of no return by the second week of the closure. Even if the strait reopens tomorrow, 4-5 months before any sense of normalcy returns. Add 6 months for full mine clearance per US Navy estimate (Apr 23) — that pushes baseline normalization into Q1 2027. — Jun Goh, Sparta Commodities — Jeff Currie (Carlyle, May 16) reframes this: the security premium is structural, not transitional. Even if Hormuz reopens, capex starvation, deglobalization, and the Mag 7's $820bn 2026 capex bid for molecules outlast the diplomatic timeline. HALO — Hard Assets, Local Operations — is the post-Hormuz regime.
recoveryClock.source: Sparta Commodities / MB Commodity Corner / Palmer Energy / US Navy mine-clearance estimate (Apr 23)

countries.notes: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report (May 13 release, data for week ending May 8): SPR = 384.1 Mb after record 8.6 Mb single-week withdrawal — beats Sept 2022's 8.4 Mb prior all-time weekly high. SPR now lowest since October 2024. Remaining inventory above the ~150 Mb operational floor leaves ~167 days at the 1.4 Mbpd IEA-committed draw rate. (The original 400 Mb authorization was framed as 'exhausted' Apr 15; new tranche now well underway — releasedMb reflects cumulative draws across both tranches.)
IEA coordinated release. 65% oil import dependency via Hormuz. Industrial production threatened.
IEA member. 70% Hormuz dependency. Refiner margins under severe pressure.
Has NOT tapped strategic reserves despite being largest importer. Massive stockpiles untouched. Reduced run rates + product export ban instead.
Limited SPR capacity. 45% Hormuz dependency. Permitted limited transits via negotiation.

sprStatus.chinaSignal: China holds ~1.3–1.4 bn barrels in strategic reserves (largest in the world) and has still NOT released any as of May 15. Per EIA expectations, China is *expanding* stockpiles by ~1 mbpd in 2026 (record 580 mt 2025 imports = +4.6% YoY). Japan and South Korea (IEA members) have released; the US drew a record 8.6 Mb single week per EIA May 13. China's continued forbearance — even with Brent recovering to $111 and a record US SPR draw rate — remains the single most important crisis-tier signal we track. When China taps its SPR, it signals peak crisis.

inflationThreshold.notes: Brent recovered to $111.04 by May 15 (+8.1% week) after testing $102 mid-week on May 6 one-page-memo optimism. WTI ~$100–104. Brent has averaged well above the $105 inflation threshold for most of the crisis — March/April CPI prints 3.2–3.5%, leaving the Fed boxed. US retail gasoline crossed $5.00/gal in many states; diesel above $5.80/gal. HFI/JPM (May): forced demand destruction running ~4.3 Mbpd, concentrated in Asian/African importers physically out of fuel. EIA May 13 record 8.6 Mb single-week SPR draw signals US can no longer slow the bleed.

tankerRates.source: Fearnleys (fearnpulse.com), S&P Global, Maritime Hub, Lloyd's List, $ECO (Okeanis) Q1 earnings call (May 14), Chris Shipping (@christankerfund, May 14), Marhelm (@MarhelmData, May 15)
tankerRates.context: Market is bifurcated — Gulf-loaded spot at extreme highs, West Africa / 1-year cover at substitute-route levels. $ECO (Okeanis Eco Tankers) Q1 call (May 14): 56% of available VLCC spot days fixed at $223,900/day; 60% of days at $187,300/day; fleet-wide blended $202,900/day. CEO Alafouzos (May 15): regrets fixing 1 VLCC at ~$90,000/day for 12 months — now eyes spot upside; 1-year VLCC cover at ~$120,000/day; West Africa→Asia spot at ~$117,500/day. The gap between Gulf-loaded ($223k) and substitute routes ($117k) measures the Hormuz premium directly. ECO acknowledged 'poor care of being trapped inside Hormuz' early in Q1 — exposure to the strait IS the asymmetric upside. CEO: 'Q2 earnings likely larger than any previous year's annual earnings.' Persian Gulf VLCC loadings remain ~zero. Many VLCCs continue to ballast to Atlantic basin loadings. War-risk premium component now ~30% above pre-crisis equivalent rates.

iranianAttacks.context: Iranian attacks on Gulf states peaked in April 2026 at 232 incidents — highest monthly total of the crisis. May tempo through May 15 (91 attacks, partial) is on track to print 180+ for the month — *higher* than April's pace in UAE-specific incidents, with May 4 being the single largest UAE strike day of the crisis. Trump's May 11 rejection of Iran's counterproposal removed the diplomatic ceiling that had briefly softened tempo in late April.
iranianAttacks.mosaicStrategyNote: Iran's 'Mosaic Strategy' — sector commanders have autonomy to launch missiles and drones without central approval. The uptick is being dismissed as decentralized action, not coordinated escalation.

refiningMargins.context: Crack spreads remain at crisis highs into May 15. Gasoline crack ~$48.5/bbl (peak $48.5 Apr 30, vs $34.2 March cycle peak), heating oil ~$67.0 (peak $67.5, vs $58.3 March peak). Cracks fattened mid-week (May 8–11) as WTI bottomed during the May 6 one-page-memo optimism window, briefly compressed on May 14 Trump-Xi diplomatic rally (gas $48.0, HO $64.2 at WTI $101.68; RBOB $3.5629/gal, HO $3.9502/gal — CME NYMEX), then re-fattened as WTI recovered to $105.42 by May 15. WTI 3-2-1 = $54.66 per Dan Tsubouchi (SAF Group, May 16): "huge crack spreads in the US, reflect the global thirst for petroleum products from what has been effectively a shut down of Persian Gulf products exports. $54.66 is a huge economic incentive for US refiners to draw more crude — a positive draw on oil prices." Still NOT a topping signal — margins must reverse before the bearish thesis activates. HFI thesis: until refining margins peak and roll over, the inventory-vs-prompt-price inverse correlation argues current oil is mispriced low.
refiningMargins.hfiThesis: If you want to know when it's time to get bearish oil, just watch refining margins. In COVID, floating storage, tanker rates, contango, and refining margins all peaked first. Then margins went negative. When they rebounded, crude rallied. This time around, a similar playbook will happen but in reverse — refining margins will be the key indicator for when the global economy cannot handle higher prices any longer.
sellTriggers: Crack spreads sustain a move back toward pre-crisis baseline (~$15 gas, ~$25 HO)
Margins go negative — refineries literally losing money on every barrel
Backwardation compresses to flat or contango
SE Asian refineries start cutting throughput rates

buyerStress.wafProgrammeDescription: WAF May programme bidding from Asian buyers remains unusually quiet — Indian and Chinese refiners largely absent from cargoes that would normally clear in the first half of the month. JH reads this as 'sitting on the sidelines hoping the Strait opens', not genuine demand softness.
buyerStress.buyerBehaviorDescription: Asian refiners running max throughput on March/April panic-bought cargoes. WTI 3-2-1 crack at $54.66 (Tsubouchi/SAF, May 15) — down from $58.28 a week earlier but still lucrative at WTI $105.42; crack briefly compressed to ~$53 on May 14 Trump-Xi summit before re-widening. Buyers can wait, and they are. The crack is the binding incentive: huge economic pull for US refiners to draw more crude → positive bid on crude prices.
buyerStress.source: JH/@CRUDEOIL231 thesis (May 6–7, 2026), Dan Tsubouchi / SAF Group (@Energy_Tidbits, May 16), refinery 3-2-1 crack via CME (RBOB+HO vs WTI), WAF programme commentary from physical traders.
buyerStress.methodology: When this lull breaks, WAF May programme bidding will spike first. Watch this for the inflection. Crack > $40 = refiners keep pulling crude (bullish-crude). Crack < $40 = product demand cracking (bearish-crude topping signal).

physicalMarketNotes.quote: 321 crack spreads −$3.62 WoW to $54.66 on 05/15. Yet WTI +$10.00 WoW to $105.42 on 05/15. $54.66 are huge crack spreads in the US and reflect the global thirst for petroleum products from the US from what has been effectively a shut down of Persian Gulf products exports. $54.66 is a huge economic incentive for US refiners to draw more crude to make big margins — a positive draw on oil prices.
physicalMarketNotes.context: Why cracks plateauing > $50 keeps the refinery-draw-on-crude bid pumping — bullish-crude reinforcement layered on the Hormuz-side supply shock.

physicalMarketNotes.quote: WAF programme is suspiciously quiet for Asian buyers. They have breathing room from panic-bought cargoes arriving in May, US + China SPR releases flooding alternatives, and 3-2-1 cracks at $54 keeping refineries running max. But this is hope-driven — when the facts don't change, they will be forced back.
physicalMarketNotes.context: The leading indicator: WAF May programme activity is the canary.

curveShape.source: ICE Brent futures curve (BZ=F prompt + long-dated approximations from physical broker quotes); Jeff Currie commentary, Carlyle (May 16 2026)
curveShape.methodology: % backwardation = (spot − 36mo) / spot × 100. Extreme backwardation = supply shock priced into spot, not into long-run expectations — implying market expects rapid normalization. When the back end stays anchored ($75 vs Russia-Ukraine $86), spot can't break out even when the physical disruption deepens.

physicalMarketNote.quote: The largest oil supply shock in history is reasonably priced into the curve, and it likely has much more to run. Percent backwardation hit an all-time high in April and remains near record today. Spot has not exceeded the Russia-Ukraine peak for one reason: the back end of the curve sits $10–$12/bbl below where it was then.
physicalMarketNote.context: Why spot looks 'cheap' even at $107 — the back end is anchoring the entire curve.

equityDisbelief.source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, S&P Capital IQ FCF estimates, Bloomberg Energy Sector Index, Jeff Currie commentary (Carlyle, May 16 2026)
equityDisbelief.methodology: Energy ÷ S&P 500 ratio is a proxy for long-dated oil. FCF yield gap = market's mispricing of the energy complex vs the broad market. At a 1,000bp+ spread, either oil must fall (spot to long-run convergence) or capital must rotate from tech to energy. Currie's thesis: the rotation is forced — $10 trillion of potential flow if Tech weight reverts from 43% toward 25%.

physicalMarketNote.quote: ExxonMobil holds 14 years of reserves. Chevron, 15. Equity prices integrate the entire forward strip. The S&P Energy ÷ S&P 500 ratio implies long-run Brent of ~$70 — below the strip at $72-75. The equity market is pricing the opposite of physical reality. The ceiling on oil is not Washington. It is Exxon's cost of capital — woefully mispriced.
physicalMarketNote.context: Why the energy equity complex is the cleanest second-derivative signal — and why the dislocation is the trade.
